summary:
Wildfires destroy ecosystems, damage economies, and create severe health hazards, yet tracking long-term burning trends is difficult. Older NASA MODIS sensors (since 2000) and newer VIIRS sensors (since 2012) report drastically different detection counts for the exact same fires, creating artificial jumps in historical data.

To solve this, we built Burning Calendar, a web app that harmonizes 26 years of MODIS and VIIRS satellite data into one consistent, continuous record. Beyond serving researchers, a core mission of the platform is to translate complex satellite telemetry into clear, intuitive insights so the general public can easily understand what the data actually means for their local environment, health, and daily lives. By comparing overlapping satellite observations over 1 km grid cells, our calibration reduces cross-sensor error from 318.5% to just 5.8% and eliminates artificial transition spikes.

Burning Calendar puts the full analysis one touch away. Choose a country, a known fire region or your own coordinates to see its month-by-month calendar, anomalies, fire season, most active years and the rain, humidity, temperature and wind behind them, with every record downloadable as CSV. Scientists get a 26-year series with no artificial jump, fire managers can see at once whether this month is unusual. Since each satellite keeps its own calibration, the record carries on as Suomi NPP and MODIS retire.
details:
1. Introduction

Active-fire hotspots from NASA MODIS (Terra/Aqua, 1 km resolution) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP, NOAA-20/21, 375 m resolution) form the longest global satellite fire record, but cannot be compared directly—VIIRS detects roughly 4× more hotspots for the same fire activity. With Suomi NPP concluding in late 2026 and MODIS retiring in 2027, historical comparisons suffer from artificial sensor-transition jumps.

Our objective was to produce a burning activity calendar from 2000 to now, for a region the user selects, that eliminates sensor-transition jumps, states its uncertainty, remains traceable to original NASA records, and translates complex satellite data into plain-language insights the public can easily understand.

Extended demo video, 3 minute (local judges) can be found in this google drive:

https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1E_kCh0gODQ7sbvm-iaNxwLk4DQIV8NAK

2. Methodology

Data. We used 80,924,077 active-fire detections from NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2) for Argentina, Brazil, India, Indonesia and Malaysia, from November 2000 to November 2026. Every record keeps its original fields. Volcanoes, static sources such as gas flares, and low-confidence detections are flagged and excluded by default, never deleted.

Cell-days. We do not count detections, because one fire is one MODIS pixel but several VIIRS pixels. Each detection is assigned to a 1 km equal-area cell, and for each satellite we count the unique cells that burned each day.

Calibration. Aqua is the reference. For every other satellite we compute a factor: the ratio of its cell-days to the reference's, on days when both were operating, for each 5° tile and month of the year. NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are calibrated against Suomi NPP and chained to Aqua, so a new satellite only needs to overlap one that is already calibrated. Overall, Terra reports 0.52 and the three VIIRS satellites 4.26 to 4.36 cell-days for every one that Aqua reports.

Harmonization and uncertainty. For each day, the cell-days of the operating satellites are summed and divided by the sum of their factors. This is a weighted average of estimates of the same quantity, not a sum of MODIS and VIIRS counts, and its unit is the Aqua-equivalent cell-day. Every value carries a 95% range from 200 bootstrap replicates covering calibration error and counting noise.

Validation. We rebuilt the record without Aqua and compared it with what Aqua observed across the 2012 transition, and we left one year at a time out of the calibration to measure the prediction error.

3. Results

Across the 2012 transition (2012–2014 against 2009–2011), Aqua observed a change of 0.88×. The harmonized record, built without Aqua, changed by 0.89×. A naive switch from MODIS to VIIRS counts gives 7.39×. In the leave-one-year-out test the median error per tile and year was 5.8%, against 318.5% without calibration. By region, the error across the transition was +0.2% for the southern Amazon, +1.9% for the Gran Chaco, +4.0% for the Cerrado, −5.2% for Sumatra and Borneo, and −8.2% for Punjab and Haryana.

The calendar itself gives clear readings. In Indonesia, 2015 was 3.5 times a normal year, the most active in the record, and July to October carry 83% of a normal year's burning. In Punjab and Haryana, burning is concentrated in October and November, the crop-residue season.

The charts and further analysis are in the web app: the calendar heat map, year stripes, the fire clock, the latest month against earlier years, the weather panels, and a chart of raw against harmonized counts for any selected region. The Method page shows the validation results and the About page lists the filter counts and limits.

4. Discussion

The harmonized record follows the independent Aqua record within about one percent overall, which shows that the jump at each sensor change can be removed with open data and a transparent method. The approach also solves a problem that is about to get worse: when MODIS ends, a record tied to MODIS ends with it, while a chained calibration only needs each new satellite to overlap with one that is already calibrated.

The method has limits, and the app states them. A hotspot is a thermal detection, not a confirmed fire, and no detection does not mean no fire, because cloud, smoke, small or short-lived fires and overpass timing all hide burning. The uncertainty range covers consistency between sensors, not fires that no satellite saw. Factors are assumed constant within their calibration window, although they drift slowly as satellite orbits change, and small regions carry more error than large ones, as the regional results show. The history is loaded for five countries, chosen because each represents a different kind of fire: peat and forest fires in Indonesia and Malaysia, deforestation fires in the Amazon, savanna fires in the Cerrado, dry-forest clearing in the Gran Chaco, and crop-residue burning in India. The whole world was too large for a free server during the hackathon, but any country's FIRMS archive can be loaded in the same way. The live map is worldwide.

5. Conclusion

Burning Calendar shows that MODIS and VIIRS hotspots can be merged into one consistent, traceable record of burning activity with a stated uncertainty. It answers the question that fire managers, scientists and the public share, whether this month is unusual, for any place with loaded history, and it is designed to keep answering it after Suomi NPP and MODIS are gone.

6. Who it is for and how it could be used

Fire and air-quality agencies can use the calendar to judge whether current burning is unusual for the season and to plan resources ahead of the months that normally burn most. Researchers get a ready-made, documented series and the calibration factors to reuse. Journalists, teachers and the public get a plain-language reading of their region. The app runs on free and open data and low-cost hosting, so an agency, university or NGO could run its own copy for its country. The next steps are to load every country, add burned-area products as an independent check, and refresh the record automatically each day.

7. Tools

Python (pandas, DuckDB, NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI), TypeScript, React, Vite, ECharts, d3-geo. The data build ran on Kaggle. The site is hosted on Modal.
